title.en: Juan Manalaksan: The Wood-Cutter and the Glass of Giants
title.zh: 胡安·馬納拉克桑：樵夫與巨人玻璃

region.en: Arayat, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省阿拉亞特（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Pampangan oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 10a 'Juan Manalaksan', eBook #8299

summary.en: The wood-cutter Juan saves the choking datu's son Pedro, and on an old woman's advice asks not for gold but for the glass Pedro keeps in his right armpit: a stick pushed through its hole summons giants who grant any wish. The charm cures a sick datu and wins Juan his daughter, but Pedro's soldiers steal wife and glass. Advised by an old mankukulam, Juan captures the king of the cats; thrown into a rat-cell, he looses the cat, and the rats buy their lives by bringing back every glass in the village — including his own, with which he orders the giants to kill Pedro and his father and bring his wife home.
summary.zh: 樵夫胡安救了噎住的達圖之子佩德羅；依老嫗之囑，他不索金銀，只要佩德羅右腋下的玻璃——穿孔小棍一捅，巨人現身有求必應。他以此符治癒達圖、娶得其女；佩德羅遣兵掠走其妻與玻璃。老巫婆指點他擒獲貓王；被囚鼠牢時他放出貓，鼠輩為保命搬來村中所有玻璃——胡安重得神符，命巨人誅佩德羅父子，迎回妻子。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan folktale recorded by Fansler from an Arayat narrator; archival record. Magic Ring/Aladdin cycle variant; the charm is a piece of glass rather than a ring, which Fansler reads as a sign of primitiveness.

passages.text: In a certain village lived a brave datu whose only son Pedro amused himself hunting deer and wild boars; nearby lived the poor wood-cutter Juan Manalaksan. Hunting on the mountain, Pedro choked on a piece of meat at their noon meal, and his father cried out loudly not knowing what to do for his dying son. Juan, cutting wood near by, ran quickly and pulled the piece of meat out of Pedro's throat, saving his life; grateful, Pedro promised a reward. On the way to the palace Juan met an old woman who warned him not to accept money or wealth, but to ask for the glass Pedro kept in his right armpit — as large as a peso, with a small hole in the centre: push a small stick through the hole, and giants who could give anything would surround him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 10 'Juan Manalaksan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Juan asked for nothing but the glass, hurried home to his starving mother, punched a small stick through the hole, and found himself surrounded by giants who fetched food at his command — though his mother ate so much that she became sick and died. In a neighboring village a datu fell ill, and proclaimed that the man who could cure him should have his daughter for a wife; the giants gave Juan medicine, the datu swallowed it and at once became well, and the next morning Juan was married and took his wife to live in his small hut in the woods.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 10 'Juan Manalaksan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day while Juan was away cutting trees, Pedro ordered soldiers to steal the wood-cutter's wife and magic glass. Going to his father-in-law for help, Juan met an old mankukulam, who told him to catch the king of the cats at a certain tree and always keep it with him. Soon after, Pedro's father commanded his soldiers to cut off the ears of all the men in the village, placing any who refused in a room full of rats; Juan refused, was seized and shut up — but he had his cat with him all the time, and as soon as the door closed he turned it loose. The rats, seeing they would all be killed, begged to serve him: 'Bring me all the glasses in this village,' said Juan, and one rat soon returned carrying the magical glass. Pushing the stick through its hole, Juan ordered the giants to kill Pedro and his father, and bring him his wife again. Thus Juan got his wife back, and they lived happily together till they died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 10 'Juan Manalaksan'; not verbatim.

title.en: Juan the Poor, Who Became Juan the King

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 10b 'Juan the Poor, who became Juan the King', eBook #8299

summary.en: Lazy Juan spares the monster in the tree he cuts, taking from its tongue a white oval stone that grants every wish; the stone builds a castle in the bay in one night and wins him the princess Maria. A defeated general hires a witch, who in the guise of Maria's old nurse steals the stone from under the sleeping princess's pillow. A huge bird strips Juan to his wood-cutter's clothes; crossing three mountains he is three times knocked down by the same cat, which he finally bags — and in the general's rat-cell the cat spares the rat-king on condition it fetch back the stolen stone. The stone destroys the castle, kills the general, frees Maria and the king, and Juan rules wisely after his father-in-law's death.
summary.zh: 懶漢胡安饒過樹中之怪，從其舌上取白色橢圓寶石，有求必應；一夜間在海灣建成城堡，娶得公主瑪利亞。敗將僱巫婆假扮乳母偷走枕下寶石；巨鳥剝去胡安華服。他三度遭同一隻貓撲倒，第三度將其裝袋；在敵國鼠牢中，貓以鼠王性命要脅取回寶石。寶石毀城堡、誅敵將、救出妻與岳王；岳王死後胡安登基，治國有道。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Clemente narrator; archival record. Magic Ring cycle variant with a wishing-stone.

passages.text: In a small hut at the edge of a forest lived a father and son so poor that the son was named Juan the Poor. Ordered to fetch firewood, the lazy boy marked every good tree, began cutting one with a hole in its trunk — and a monster came out of the hole as soon as the tree fell. Juan raised his axe: 'Good sir, forbear, And my life spare, If you wish a happy life And, besides, a pretty wife,' chanted the monster, and told him to take from the middle of its tongue a white oval stone from which he could ask for and get whatever he wanted. Juan tested the charm by summoning men who cut down trees and carried the wood to his house, then hurried home and lay down again behind the fireplace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 10 'Juan the Poor'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Remembering the pretty wife, Juan went to the king's palace to ask for his daughter's hand; the king, scorning the rustic suitor, demanded a castle built in the middle of the bay within three days, on pain of losing his head. Two days Juan did nothing; at midnight of the third he bade his stone build a fort in the middle of the bay, and the next morning, dressed like a prince, presented it as the king bathed to the sound of cannon-shots. He married the princess Maria. When war broke out he led his father-in-law's army and conquered the mighty enemy with the stone's help — and the defeated general, never beaten before, offered half his property to anyone who could get Juan's power for him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 10 'Juan the Poor'; not verbatim.

passages.text: A witch who knew Juan's secret flew to the general, then to Juan's house one hot afternoon, smiling at Maria: 'Do you not recognize me, pretty Maria? I am the one who nursed you when you were a baby.' The princess believed her, treated her kindly, and lay down to a siesta; fanning her to sleep, the witch took from under the pillow the magical stone Juan had forgotten to take hunting, and rewarded herself with half the general's riches. As Juan enjoyed his hunt, a huge bird swooped down and seized his horse and clothes, his inner garments changing back into his old wood-cutter's clothes — an ill omen that sent him hastening home on foot to find house and palace deserted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 10 'Juan the Poor'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Concluding that the general had his stone, Juan crossed three mountains toward the general's country — and each time a cat came running after him and knocked him down. He dashed out its life against a rock twice, but the same cat tumbled him a third time; filled with curiosity, he caught it and put it in his bag. At the castle he begged a mouthful of rice; recognized, he was thrown into the cell of rats. Remembering his cat, he let it loose, and it killed all the rats except their king. 'Now you shall die if you do not promise to get for Juan his magical stone, which your master has stolen,' said the cat — and the rat-king ran quickly to the general's room and took the stone from the table. Juan then said to his stone, 'Pretty stone, destroy this house with the general and his subjects, and release my father-in-law and wife from their prison.' The earth trembled, the castle was destroyed, the general and his subjects dead, and his wife and father-in-law free. After the death of the king, Juan ascended to the throne and ruled wisely, living long happily with his lovely wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 10 'Juan the Poor'; not verbatim.

title.en: Lucas the Strong: The Golden Carriage and the Four Companions
title.zh: 力士盧卡斯：金車與四同伴

region.en: Laguna lake region, Luzon, Philippines (Tagalog narrator's home)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋拉古納湖區（他加祿敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 11a 'Lucas the Strong', eBook #8299

summary.en: Lazy Lucas bites off the end of a boa-constrictor's tail — the reptile's seat of strength — and becomes the strongest man in his barrio. When the king promises the princess to whoever gives him a golden carriage, his hardworking brothers fail and spurn a begging leper, but Lucas shares his meat with her and receives carriage, clothes, and shoes from her promise. On the road he wrestles four prodigies into his service: Runner, Sharpshooter, Farsight, and Blower. Set against the king's giant messenger for a bottle of the water of youth, Runner is drugged with a gold ring in his bottle, but Farsight spies, Blower blows the giant to the eighth mountain, and Sharpshooter shoots the bottle's head to wake Runner — Lucas marries the princess.
summary.zh: 懶漢盧卡斯咬下蟒蛇尾尖——蛇之力源——成為村中最強者。國王懸賞金車以聘公主；兩位勤勞兄長掘金失敗且拒施捨癩婦，盧卡斯分肉與之，遂得金車、衣履。途中他以摔跤收服四人：飛毛腿、神射手、千里眼、大風。國王令巨人與之競取『不老泉』；巨人以金戒使飛毛腿昏睡，千里眼偵察，大風將巨人吹回第八座山，神射手射穿瓶頭喚醒飛毛腿——盧卡斯終娶公主。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Macasaet narrator; archival record. Skilful-Companions cycle; the boa's tail-tip as seat of strength is a local belief.

passages.text: A man had three sons — Juan, Pedro, and Lucas — his wife dying young; Juan and Pedro were hard workers, but Lucas was lazy, rambling about the forests and river-banks looking for guavas and birds' nests. One day in the woods Lucas saw a boa-constrictor and knew that this reptile carried the centre of its strength in the horny appendage at the end of its tail; wishing to become strong, for the men of strength in his barrio were the most influential, he approached the snake like a cat, bit off the end of its tail with his sharp teeth, and ran away with all his might. The boa followed but could not overtake him, for it had lost its strength, and Lucas soon became the strongest man in his barrio, defeating the man who used to be the Hercules of the place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 11 'Lucas the Strong'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The king proclaimed that whoever gave him a carriage made of gold should have the princess for his wife. Juan dug for gold on a mountain and refused his lunch to an old leper with her child — 'Go away! You are very dirty' — and after three weeks gave up; Pedro fared no better and was also unkind to the old leper. When the woman begged of Lucas, he gave her half his meat, and she promised him not only the golden carriage but a pair of shoes, a coat, and trousers. Nine days she did not come, and Lucas repented his kindness — until she appeared, told him what he had been thinking, and vanished; the next day he saw the golden carriage drawn by a pair of fine fat horses, with the clothes inside, and she showed him how to wear them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 11 'Lucas the Strong'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Driving toward the palace, Lucas met and wrestled into his service four prodigies: Runner, son of the good runner; Sharpshooter, son of the famous shooter; Farsight, son of the great Sharp-Eyes; and Blower, son of the great blower. At the palace the king set a final challenge: fetch a bottle of the water that gives youth and health from the foot of the seventh mountain, faster than his messenger — a giant — or lose his head. Runner ran with all his might and caught up with the giant, but the giant secretly put a gold ring in Runner's bottle to make him sleep. Farsight saw Runner sleeping and the giant very near the city; Blower blew the giant back to the eighth mountain; Sharpshooter shot the head of the bottle so that Runner woke up, ran and got the precious water, and arrived in the city in twelve hours. Lucas presented the water to the king, and the monarch was obliged to accept the young man as his son-in-law — though the third day after the nuptials the giant reached the palace claiming a heavy wind had blown him back to the eighth mountain.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 11 'Lucas the Strong'; not verbatim.
